rationale: Matthew’s mustard plant “becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches” (13:32, BSB); Nebuchadnezzar’s dream-tree has branches where “the birds of the air nested” (Daniel 4:12, repeated in Daniel’s interpretation at 4:21, BSB). In Greek, the text Bible Hub serves as Swete’s shares Matthew’s “the birds of the air” (ta peteina tou ouranou) but uses a different verb (enosseuon), while the Greek Daniel served by Blue Letter Bible has “in its branches” and Matthew’s verb (kateskenoun) at 4:21 but a different word for birds (ornea). The Pulpit Commentary says to compare Daniel 4:12 and 21 “for both thought and language,” Scofield’s notes say the figure “is drawn from Dan 4:20-22,” and Ellicott compares “the imagery of Ezekiel 31:3; Daniel 4:10” (all via Bible Hub). Graded plausible, not strong, on the precedent of conn-matt9-sheep-ezekiel34: there is no citation formula, and the same image of birds nesting in a great tree’s branches also stands at Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6, so the wording cannot single out Daniel. The commentators also differ over what the echo would imply, since Daniel’s tree is a king’s empire that is cut down; that dispute is reported in the lesson and not settled by this row.
